Exam Essentials.title: 60 items, 120 minutes, 720 to pass
Exam Essentials.desc: Single best answer from four options, scored on a 100–1000 scale with a 720 cut, across five domains weighted 27%, 20%, 20%, 18% and 15%. That is two minutes an item, and there is no penalty for guessing — a blank and a wrong answer score identically.
Exam Essentials.note: Never leave an item unanswered. If one is eating the clock, record your best elimination and move; the 27% domain rewards those minutes far more than one stubborn question does.

Exam Essentials.title: Foundations asks whether you can build it
Exam Essentials.desc: This exam tests design and construction: choosing a pattern, writing a tool schema the model actually selects correctly, structuring a prompt, configuring Claude Code for a team, keeping a long conversation coherent. It does not test procurement, regulatory regimes, cost cases or stakeholder management.
Exam Essentials.note: An option that answers a governance or business-case question the stem never asked is a distractor. Stay on the mechanism and on what the system will actually do.

Exam Essentials.title: Guarantee goes in code, tendency in the prompt
Exam Essentials.desc: An instruction in a prompt is followed most of the time. A precondition inside the tool, an allow-list, or a hook that blocks the call is followed every time. Anything irreversible, financial or safety-relevant belongs on the deterministic side of that line.
Exam Essentials.note: The stem gives it away with "usually" or "occasionally the agent still…". A better-worded instruction is almost never the key; the enforcement point is.

Exam Essentials.title: Structural signals beat parsed prose
Exam Essentials.desc: The platform gives you fields designed to be branched on — `stop_reason`, `isError`, a schema-validated tool input. Assistant text is a probabilistic artefact. Any control flow that depends on the model phrasing something a particular way eventually meets a paraphrase and breaks.
Exam Essentials.note: Options that string-match the assistant's output, or that ask the model to emit a sentinel phrase, are wrong even when the sentinel is well chosen.

Exam Essentials.title: Four scenarios out of eight
Exam Essentials.desc: Each sitting draws four scenarios from a pool covering customer support, Claude Code development, multi-agent research, developer tooling, CI integration, structured extraction, conversational patterns and agentic tooling. The same handful of mechanisms recurs across all of them in different costume.
Exam Essentials.note: Read past the setting. A refund ceiling in a support agent and a merge gate in CI are the same question about deterministic enforcement.

Exam Essentials.title: "MOST appropriate" means find the constraint
Exam Essentials.desc: Several options will be defensible practice. One responds to what this scenario actually pins down — a latency requirement, an irreversible action, a config that must be shared, a document that will not fit. The constraint is usually stated in a single clause of the stem.
Exam Essentials.note: If your elimination sounds like "that's generally weaker", you have the wrong answer. It should sound like "that ignores the fact this tool moves money".

Exam Essentials.title: The simplest mechanism that meets the need
Exam Essentials.desc: A fixed pipeline before an agentic loop. One agent with good tools before a coordinator and subagents. A schema before a validation service. Extra machinery has to be forced by something in the stem, not chosen because it is more capable.
Exam Essentials.note: The most elaborate option is a distractor more often than a key. Ask which sentence in the stem the extra complexity is answering; if none, drop it.

Exam Essentials.title: Fix the cause, not the symptom
Exam Essentials.desc: Repeated tool calls point at incomplete tool output. Wrong tool selection points at overlapping descriptions. Drifting format points at a missing example. This bank consistently rewards the option that repairs the input to the model over the one that applies more pressure to the model.
Exam Essentials.note: "Use a more capable model" and "state it more emphatically in the system prompt" are the two most reliable wrong answers in the whole bank.

Exam Essentials.title: Absent, empty and failed are different
Exam Essentials.desc: "No results found" is not "the lookup failed", and neither is "the field was not present in the document". Zero is a value; null is an absence. A system that collapses these states forces the model to guess which one happened, and it guesses wrong.
Exam Essentials.note: When a stem describes an agent misreading a result, check first whether the tool contract or the schema can even express the distinction it needed to make.

Exam Essentials.title: Ask what each component can actually see
Exam Essentials.desc: The Messages API keeps no state between calls. A subagent inherits nothing from its parent. A second Claude Code instance shares no reasoning with the first. A CI run starts blank. Most failures in this bank trace to context someone assumed would carry across a boundary.
Exam Essentials.note: Trace the boundary before answering: who assembled this context, and does the component that needs it actually receive it inside its own request?

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: The agentic loop contract
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: Send the full history with tools attached, read `stop_reason`, and while it is `tool_use`, append the assistant turn containing the `tool_use` block plus a user turn containing the matching `tool_result`, then send everything again. The API holds no session state, so the history is your job.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: N `tool_use` blocks in one assistant message must be answered by N `tool_result` blocks in **one** user message, matched by `tool_use_id`. Splitting them across messages is a 400.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Fixed pipeline versus agentic loop
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: A fixed pipeline runs steps you wrote in an order you chose. An agentic loop lets the model pick the next action from what it has seen so far. Choose fixed when the steps are knowable in advance; choose model-driven only when the next step genuinely depends on the previous result.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: Predictable, repeatable work — reviews, migrations, extraction runs — is a pipeline. If the stem can enumerate the steps, the answer is not an autonomous agent.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Chaining, routing and parallelisation
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: Chaining runs focused steps in sequence so each gets undivided attention, avoiding the dilution of dumping everything into one call. Routing classifies the input first and dispatches to a specialised handler. Parallelisation either splits distinct subtasks across workers (sectioning) or runs the same task repeatedly and combines verdicts (voting).
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: At the finest grain, parallelisation is emitting several independent `tool_use` blocks in one turn. Latency tracks the number of loop iterations, not the number of tool calls.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Orchestrator–workers and hub-and-spoke
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: A coordinator decomposes the task at run time, delegates to specialised subagents, aggregates their results and handles their failures. All inter-agent traffic passes through the hub, giving one observable trace. It buys context isolation, scoped toolsets and parallelism; it costs tokens and coordination complexity.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: If every subagent succeeded but the report is incomplete, the fault is the coordinator's decomposition, not the workers. Coverage failures are assignment failures.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Subagents inherit nothing
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: A delegated task begins with only the prompt you hand it. It cannot see the parent conversation, another subagent's findings, or anything from an earlier delegation. The delegation prompt has to carry the goal, the full inputs, the output contract and the quality bar.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: Parallel subagents need disjoint, exhaustive slices with the exclusions stated explicitly. Because they cannot see each other, overlap and duplicated work is the default outcome.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Bound the loop, and make failure legible
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: An iteration cap is a circuit breaker, not a completion condition — a task that finishes in three steps should not burn twelve, and one needing twelve should not be silently truncated. When the breaker trips or a tool fails, the model needs an error it can actually act on.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: Two half-answers appear together: a cap with an opaque failure, and a good error message with no cap. The design needs both, and the key says so.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Handoffs are structured payloads
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: When one agent hands work to another, or to a human, the transfer needs an identifier, the reason, what was already attempted, the evidence gathered and a recommended next action — as fields. A summary dropped into prose gets lost, and the receiver repeats work the sender already did.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: The diagnostic signal is the receiver asking for something the sender already held. That is a handoff-contract problem, not an effort problem.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Hooks intercept the tool boundary
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: A `PreToolUse` hook sees a call before it executes and can block or redirect it — a refund ceiling, a required prior step, a protected path. A `PostToolUse` hook sees the result before the model does and can normalise or annotate it. Both run deterministically.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: Reconciling inconsistent date or currency formats coming from several MCP servers is `PostToolUse` work. Stopping an action that breaks a business rule is `PreToolUse` work.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Evaluator–optimiser: generate then critique
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: One call produces, a second critiques against stated criteria, the first revises. It pays where criteria are articulable and iteration measurably helps — writing to a rubric, code that must pass tests. It requires a bounded iteration count and an explicit stopping condition.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: The critic must judge against written criteria, not general quality. An unbounded critique loop with a vague rubric is a cost incident, and the bank treats it as one.

Agent Architecture & Orchestration.title: Resume, fork, or start fresh
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.desc: Resuming continues a session with its accumulated context, which is right while that context is still true. Forking branches from a shared point so two approaches can be developed and compared independently. Starting fresh with a written summary is right once the underlying files have moved on.
Agent Architecture & Orchestration.note: "The codebase has changed since that session" is the signal for a fresh session plus a summary. Resuming would carry stale file reads forward as if they were current.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Explicit criteria, and what to ignore
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: "Be conservative, report only real issues" is unverifiable and every run interprets it differently. A numbered list of conditions that qualify, paired with an equally explicit list of things not to flag, turns a judgement call into a decision procedure the model can apply consistently.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: Criteria generalise; examples illustrate the boundary. Decision rules want both — the rule stated, then a near-miss pair showing which side each case falls on.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Structured output through `tool_use`
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Defining a JSON Schema and having the model fill it is the reliable route to machine-readable output: no missing braces, no trailing commas, required fields present. It guarantees the shape only. Every value inside can still be wrong, so validation in code is not optional.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: "Ask the model to reply in valid JSON" is the weakest option available. Separate syntax errors, which the schema eliminates, from semantic errors, which it cannot touch.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Examples come from the messy tail
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Two to four examples drawn from the awkward cases — the ambiguous document, the missing field, the unusual phrasing — teach far more than a dozen clean ones. Examples demonstrate format and decision logic at the same time, which is why they beat prose describing the same rule.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: When adding examples stops helping, diagnose the remaining errors rather than adding more. Flattening returns mean the surviving failures have a different cause.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Show the model a null result
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: If every example in the prompt contains findings, the model learns that finding something is the expected output, and it will manufacture one on a clean input. Including at least one example whose correct answer is an empty result teaches that returning nothing is a legitimate answer.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: "It reports problems in code that has none" is exactly this gap. The fix is a no-findings example, not a sterner instruction to be conservative.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: `required` invites fabrication
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: A required field must be filled, so when the source does not contain it the model supplies something plausible instead. Reserve `required` for information that is genuinely always present, and make everything else nullable so the model has an honest way to report absence.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: For collections, keep the field required and let it be an empty array. That preserves the difference between "looked and found none" and "did not look".

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Model the shape, normalise the values
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Repeated records belong in an array of typed objects, never parallel arrays or a delimited string that permits invalid states. Enums want an `other` plus a detail field and an `unclear` value, so unexpected cases are captured rather than forced into the nearest bucket.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: State normalisation rules in the prompt — dates as ISO, amounts as number plus currency code. A union-typed field usually signals a modelling error, not genuine variety.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Validate in code, retry with the error
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Extraction is a loop: extract, validate against the schema and the business rules, then on failure re-prompt with the original source, the previous output and the specific discrepancy. "Total is 150 but the line items sum to 145" gives the model something to correct; "try again" does not.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: Retry fixes format, placement and arithmetic errors. It cannot conjure information the source never contained — those cases need routing to review, not another attempt.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Over-strict validation is a failure too
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: A rule that rejects valid output costs a retry and then a human's attention, and enough of them drown the review queue. Measure precision per rule — what share of its rejections were genuine. A rule that is usually wrong should be repaired or removed, not tolerated.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: Cut review volume by improving accuracy on the fields that trigger it, never by routing fewer items or capping the queue. A cap hides the failures instead of fixing them.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: A second pass must be independent
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Another review pass adds value only if it differs in remit, in input, or in independence from the first. An instance that generated the work is a weak critic of it, because it still carries the reasoning that produced the flaw. Identical passes duplicate findings rather than adding any.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: Judge an extra pass by unique true positives minus the noise it adds, not by comment count. Shared standards are fine; shared generation reasoning is the contamination.

Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.title: Batch versus synchronous processing
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.desc: Asynchronous batch trades latency for cost on work where nobody is waiting — overnight reports, bulk document runs, periodic audits. It carries no latency guarantee and each request is single-shot, so a multi-turn tool-using conversation cannot run that way. A `custom_id` ties each result back to its input.
Prompt Engineering & Structured Output.note: Plan against the maximum window rather than the typical case, and sample-test a small batch first — small batches give earlier signal and contain the blast radius.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Project scope versus personal scope
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: `.claude/` inside the repository is shared through version control and applies to everyone who clones it. `~/.claude/` in your home directory is personal and follows you across projects. Which directory a file sits in decides who gets the behaviour, and whether a teammate can reproduce it.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: This single rule resolves a large share of the domain. "A new joiner is not picking up the conventions" nearly always means they live in the user-level file.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: CLAUDE.md is a context budget
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: Its contents load into context on every request, so each line competes with the actual task. It is for durable, actionable conventions Claude must follow — commands, standards, constraints — not architecture narrative or onboarding prose. Human-facing explanation belongs in the README.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: Stale entries are worse than missing ones: they dilute the live rules and actively mislead. Pruning when the code changes is part of owning the file.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Where a convention should live
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: Memory layers from organisation-managed and user level down through project and directory-level files, with the more specific file taking precedence and subdirectory files loading when Claude works in that directory. `@path` imports pull in shared fragments, resolved relative to the importing file, to a limited recursion depth.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: Universal and short goes in `CLAUDE.md`. Detailed but universal goes in an unscoped rule file. Detailed and specific to certain files goes in a path-scoped rule.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Path-scoped rules load conditionally
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: A rule file under `.claude/rules/` carrying `paths` globs in its frontmatter loads only when Claude touches a matching file, so test conventions reach test files without consuming context during unrelated work. One rule file can carry several globs and follow a concern across services.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: A glob matching everything is a no-op with extra indirection. Overlapping globs with contradictory content are the trap — consolidate, or phrase one as an explicit exception.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Slash commands and skills
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: A reusable procedure stored as a file becomes an invocable `/name`. The older form is a single markdown file under `commands/`; the current form is a directory under `skills/` holding a `SKILL.md`, which can also carry frontmatter and supporting files. Both are shared or personal by location.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: Shared commands need distinct names and when-to-use descriptions. A personal variant that shadows a team command creates behaviour nobody else can reproduce.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: `allowed-tools` grants least capability
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: Frontmatter can restrict a skill or command to the tools it genuinely needs, so a review procedure that only reads cannot write or delete. Prefer a purpose-built tool over shell access; where shell access is unavoidable, scope it to specific commands rather than granting it wholesale.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: The wrong answers grant broad capability and rely on instructions to restrain it. Capability never granted cannot be misused; capability merely discouraged can.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: `context: fork` isolates the noise
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: A skill declared to run forked executes in its own context and returns only its result to the main session, so a wide search or a verbose audit does not fill the parent's window with intermediate output. The return payload then becomes the entire interface between the two.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: Scope the return to the conclusion plus the minimum evidence needed to act on it. Handing the full transcript back defeats the only reason to fork.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Planning mode versus direct execution
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: Planning mode investigates with read-only tools and produces a plan you approve before anything changes. It earns its cost when the change is large, the codebase unfamiliar, or several approaches are viable. A single-file fix with a clear stack trace does not need it.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: Consequence outranks diff size. A three-line change on an authentication path gets planned; a hundred-line mechanical rename does not.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Correct the plan, not the output
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: Iterative refinement works when feedback names the specific defect and the expected behaviour, ideally as a concrete failing case. Naming an area — "the error handling feels off" — invites redesign of things that were fine. Where a plan exists, correcting the plan is far cheaper than correcting the implementation.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: If plans keep missing constraints Claude could not have known, the fix is upstream: have it interview you for what it needs before it plans anything.

Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.title: Headless runs in CI
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.desc: `-p` (or `--print`) runs non-interactively — it takes the prompt, writes to stdout and exits, which is the only workable shape inside a pipeline. `--output-format json` makes the result parseable, so a job can turn findings into inline comments rather than a wall of text.
Claude Code Configuration & Workflows.note: A review bot lives or dies on false positives. State what to ignore as explicitly as what to report; high comment volume means over-broad criteria, not thoroughness.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: The description is the selection mechanism
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: The model chooses a tool by reading its description, so that text must state what the tool does, what it returns, the accepted input formats with examples, its constraints, and when to use it instead of the nearest similar tool. "Retrieves customer information" conveys almost nothing.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: When the model picks the wrong tool, the fix is the description and the schema. "Add an instruction to the system prompt" and "use a stronger model" are the standing distractors.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Name the tool for its boundary
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: The name is the first and cheapest selection signal. Verb-plus-object names that reveal scope — `lookup_order_status`, `issue_partial_refund` — carry information. `process_data`, `handle_request` and `analyze_content` waste it and leave the model disambiguating from prose alone.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: Two tools whose descriptions could be swapped without either becoming false will be confused. Fix it by naming the contrast with the nearest alternative in both.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Scope tools to the agent's role
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: Selection reliability falls as the toolset grows, especially with near-duplicates. Give each agent the tools its role actually needs plus a small number of narrow cross-role utilities, and relocate the rest rather than deleting them. Narrow and purpose-built beats broad and general.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: "Give the subagent everything so it never gets stuck" is a standing wrong answer. Grant a narrow tool for the common case and route the tail through the coordinator.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: `tool_choice`: auto, any, forced
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: `auto` lets the model decide whether to call anything, and is the default for agent loops. `any` requires some tool call, which is how you guarantee structured output. Naming a specific tool requires that one, which is how you guarantee a mandatory first step such as validation.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: `any` inside an agentic loop prevents termination: the model can never produce the plain text answer that ends the turn, so it keeps calling tools.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Errors need `isError` and a payload
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: A failing tool sets `isError: true` and returns something the agent can reason from: what failed, whether it is retryable, what was attempted, any partial results, and what to try instead. "Operation failed" leaves the model nothing, so it retries blindly or abandons the task.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: Separate the audiences inside the payload — a user-safe message, model-facing recovery flags, internal diagnostics. Leaking a stack trace into the user-safe field is a wrong option.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Error category decides retryability
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: Transient failures — timeouts, rate limits, upstream unavailability — are worth retrying after the indicated delay. Validation errors need the input corrected, not repeated. Permission refusals and business-rule limits are deterministic: the identical call fails identically forever, so retrying is waste and escalation is the answer.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: The tool must carry the category; the agent cannot infer it from a message string. A rate limit is transient, a refund ceiling is not, and both read as "denied".

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: State-changing tools must be idempotent
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: Assume every tool that writes, pays, sends or files will eventually be called twice — through a retry, a re-planned step, or a resumed session. An idempotency key plus a deduplication check makes the second call a no-op instead of a second refund.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: Any option that adds retry logic in front of a mutating tool without addressing duplication is incomplete, however carefully the backoff is described.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Built-in tools: search before you read
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: `Grep` searches file contents, `Glob` finds files by name pattern, `Read` opens a specific file once search has narrowed the field, and `Edit` makes a targeted change. Opening files speculatively to find something burns context that one search would have saved.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: Agents drift toward built-in tools over MCP tools with similar names, so an MCP tool's description must say what unique data or context the built-in cannot provide.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: MCP resources are catalogues, not actions
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: An MCP server exposes tools the model invokes to act, resources the client can read for context — schemas, reference data, catalogues, documentation — and prompt templates a user invokes. A resource hands the agent a map so it does not need exploratory calls to discover what exists.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: Exposing read-only reference data as a tool is the common design error: it forces a round trip and spends context on something the client could simply attach.

Tool Design & MCP Integration.title: Where an MCP server is configured
Tool Design & MCP Integration.desc: A project-scoped server lives in `.mcp.json` at the repository root and is committed, so every contributor has it on clone. Local and user-scoped servers are registered in `~/.claude.json` and stay private. Secrets go in environment variables referenced from the file, never in the file.
Tool Design & MCP Integration.note: "Everyone must run a setup script first" signals the wrong scope. Project configuration should be live on clone; supplying credentials as environment variables is the one legitimate setup step.

Context Management & Reliability.title: The window is the entire memory
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Everything the model can use on a call is inside that call: system prompt, tool definitions, the whole message history, and every tool result accumulated so far. Nothing persists server-side between requests, so context management is a design activity rather than something the platform does for you.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Cost scales with that re-sent prefix, which is what prompt caching addresses. Dropping history to save tokens is the wrong lever — cache the stable prefix instead.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Curate by relevance, not by position
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Trimming the oldest turns discards whatever was established early — the account number, the agreed constraint, the decision made in turn three. Instead extract the facts that must survive into a persistent block your code maintains and re-injects, and trim verbose tool results field by field.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Group the facts by topic, mark their scope, and prune resolved ones — the block only works while it stays small. Keep the inputs as well as the conclusions drawn from them.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Summarisation loses specifics first
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Compaction is lossy in a predictable direction. Exact numbers, dates, identifiers and named constraints degrade into "about", "recently" and "a few", while narrative survives intact — which is precisely backwards from what downstream steps need in order to act.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Test a summarisation step by checking whether specific values survive it. Precise values belong in a code-maintained facts block that never passes through the summariser.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Durable instructions live outside the turn
Context Management & Reliability.desc: An instruction given in turn two competes with everything said since and will not reliably govern turn forty. Anything that must hold for the whole conversation belongs in the system prompt or in a persistent block the code re-injects; the conversation carries turn-specific requests.
Context Management & Reliability.note: "The agent followed the rule at first and then stopped" is this failure exactly. The answer is to relocate the instruction, not to repeat it more often.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Keep the investigation out of the main context
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Exploring a large codebase produces far more output than conclusion. Search to narrow before reading, filter irrelevant content when you construct the input rather than instructing the model to ignore it, and delegate wide searches so only the summary comes back.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Delegation raises total tokens while lowering main-session context — that is the trade, and it is usually worth it. Externalise findings to a file, then actually read the file back.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Escalation needs stated criteria
Context Management & Reliability.desc: An agent escalates well only when the triggers are written down: an explicit request for a human, a value above a threshold, an unrecognised failure category, repeated unsuccessful attempts. "Escalate if you cannot help" leaves the boundary to be reinvented in every conversation.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Examine re-routed escalations for what they share. They mean either the routing criteria are wrong or the handoff was incomplete, and those have different fixes.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Clarify only what is underdetermined
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Asking the user is right when the request genuinely admits several actions with different consequences. It is wrong when the policy was already stated and the agent simply failed to apply it — that reads as incompetence and destroys first-contact resolution.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Conditional is not the same as ambiguous. If the stem contains the rule, the answer is to apply it, not to ask the customer which branch they would prefer.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Fail loudly, define degraded mode
Context Management & Reliability.desc: A failing component must propagate its failure type, the attempt count, any partial results and the viable alternatives. Silent suppression and aborting the whole workflow are both wrong. Decide in advance which components are critical and which optional, and what the output looks like without each one.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Annotate partial coverage in the result itself. A visible gap is worth far more than confident prose that quietly omits what could not be gathered.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Calibrate the threshold from both sides
Context Management & Reliability.desc: A confidence threshold has two error rates: items above it that turned out wrong, and items below it that a reviewer confirmed were already correct. Tuning on one direction alone always looks like progress. Review outcomes are labelled data — use them to place the line.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Carry a confidence score only where routing actually varies on it. Fields that are always automated, or always reviewed, do not need one attached.

Context Management & Reliability.title: Provenance is structural, not stylistic
Context Management & Reliability.desc: Attribution survives only when carried as fields — claim, source, location, date — from extraction through synthesis to output. Asking for citations at the end fails, because summarisation has already severed each statement from where it came from.
Context Management & Reliability.note: Mark inferences as inferences and cite the inputs they rest on. Conflicting sources get annotated with attribution and dates and escalated, never silently resolved in favour of one.
